# sleep-watch

tells a bot when the machine went to sleep, and on linux also right before it does. a bot that holds money (a lightning node) must not just keep going after a sleep, cuz another device might have taken over in the meantime. so the bot stops, and after waking up datashell first checks with the other devices before it starts the bot again

```js
const sleep_watch = require('sleep-watch')
const watch = sleep_watch({ on_sleep, before_sleep })

// after waking up, gap = how long the process was frozen (ms), at = Date.now() when the late tick came
function on_sleep ({ gap, at }) { restart_after_checking_other_devices() }
// linux only, right before sleeping. call done() when the bot is stopped, the machine waits for that (5s max)
function before_sleep (done) { stop_bot().then(done) }

watch.stop()
```

the options are `interval` (100ms) and `limit` (2000ms). a tick that comes more than `limit` after the one before counts as a sleep

## how it knows

- **after waking up, everywhere** (bare, node, browsers, any os, only tried bare and node on linux so far). a timer ticks every 100ms. while the machine sleeps the whole process is frozen, so the next tick comes way too late and `Date.now()` jumped. thats `on_sleep`
- **before sleeping, linux on bare**. systemd-logind sends `PrepareForSleep (true,)` right before suspend / hibernate and `(false,)` after waking up. we listen with `gdbus monitor`, and we hold a "delay" lock with `systemd-inhibit`, so logind waits for us before it sleeps (`InhibitDelayMaxSec`, 5s by default). `done()` releases the lock, after waking up we take a new one. thats `before_sleep`
- the lock is held by a `cat` that `systemd-inhibit` runs, so it goes away when we close its stdin, and also when our process crashes or gets killed (`kill -9` tested), it never blocks sleep forever

## what it cant do

- `on_sleep` only comes after waking up, not before
- a big clock change, or blocking the event loop for longer than `limit`, looks the same as a sleep
- `before_sleep` needs bare, `systemd-inhibit` and `gdbus` (linux with systemd). without them it quietly only does the time check. linux without systemd usually has elogind, which should send the same signal, but the tools may be named differently, not tried
- nothing before sleeping on mac and windows yet, they need native code (IOKit on mac, `WM_POWERBROADCAST` on windows)
- `systemctl suspend -i` ignores locks, an empty battery or pulling the plug sends nothing, and if the bot needs more than 5s logind sleeps anyway. in all these cases only `on_sleep` notices, after waking up
- it starts system tools (with `bare-subprocess`), thats a powerful capability, so its only for datashell itself, apps dont get it

## tested

`node lib/node_modules/sleep-watch/test.js` freezes node and bare processes with SIGSTOP for 3s (looks the same as a sleep from inside) and checks the gap. `before_sleep` needs a real suspend, so its not in that test, for that run `bare lib/node_modules/sleep-watch/test.js real`, suspend, wake up and look at the output. works with a real `systemctl suspend` on my laptop too
